Foundations of Structured Programming

01
C O N C E P T
What is structured programming?
A discipline for writing programs as a clear
hierarchy of blocks, using only three control
structures — no tangled jumps.
Single entry, single exit
Each block is entered and left at one point —
easy to reason about.
No arbitrary goto
Replace jumps with loops and conditionals.
Readable & testable
Structure mirrors the logic, so bugs are easier to
isolate.
The three building blocks
Sequence
A
B
C
Do A, then B, then C — in
order.
Selection
cond?
then else
Choose a path: if / else,
switch.
Iteration
cond?
body
loop while true
Repeat while a condition
holds: for, while.
06
C O N C E P T · D E C O M P O S I T I O N
From problem to program
Top-down decomposition
1Start with the whole task
State what the program must do as one
goal.
2Break into sub-problems
Split into independent responsibilities.
3Refine into functions
Each leaf becomes a small, named
function.
4Group related functions
Cohesive functions form a module.
engine_monitor
acquire()
read_adc
read_rpm
process()
to_celsius
check_limit
report()
log_line
raise_alert
Each leaf is small enough to write and test on its own.
07
M O D U L A R D E S I G N
Functions: the unit of decomposition
One job each — A function should do exactly one thing,
and its name should say what.
Small & readable — Aim for a screenful; extract helpers
when it grows.
Clear parameters — Pass what it needs; avoid hidden
global state.
Meaningful returns — Return results or status codes the
caller can act on.
sensor.h — a good signature
/* Name + types = a mini contract */
int sensor_is_over_limit(int16_t celsius);
/* caller knows: input, output,
and that nothing else changes */
A clear signature tells the caller everything — without reading the
body.
08
D E S I G N Q U A L I T Y
Cohesion & coupling
Two forces that decide how maintainable your modules are.
AIM HIGH
High cohesion
Everything in a module belongs together and serves one
clear purpose.
One responsibility per module
Related data + operations grouped
Easy to name in one phrase
AIM LOW
Low coupling
Modules depend on each other as little as possible — only
through interfaces.
Talk via headers, not internals
Few, narrow dependencies
Swap implementations freely
09
D E S I G N Q U A L I T Y · E X A M P L E
The same job, two ways
One tiny sensor task — read a temperature and act on it — written two ways.
AVOID Low cohesion · high coupling
/* one blob: HW + math + I/O + alert */
int g_raw; FILE *g_log; /* globals */
void do_all(void) {
g_raw = read_adc();
float c = g_raw * 0.1f - 40;
fprintf(g_log, "%f", c);
if (c > 85) email(boss, c);
}
One function does every job through shared globals — any change risks
breaking the rest.
PREFER High cohesion · low coupling
/* each module: one job, talk via .h */
int16_t c = sensor_read(); /* sensor.c */
log_write(c); /* logger.c */
if (alert_over_limit(c)) /* policy.c */
notify(c); /* notifier.c */
Four focused modules meet only through headers — each can be tested or
swapped on its own.

sensor.h

The promise you keep
Implementation — the HOW
sensor.c
Function definitions (bodies)
static internal helpers
Private file-scope data
Free to change anytime
Program to the interface
main.c
the caller
sensor.h
the contract
sensor.c
the details

M U L T I - F I L E M E C H A N I C S
Header files vs source files
.h — Header
Declarations & shared promises
P U T H E R E
#include guard
typedefs & struct layouts
function prototypes
extern constants
callable macros
! No function bodies or definitions here.
.c — Source
Definitions & private logic
P U T H E R E
function definitions
static helper functions
file-scope (static) data
local macros
#include of its own .h
! definition, in exactly .c file.
13
M U L T I - F I L E M E C H A N I C S
Anatomy of a header: include guards
sensor.h
#ifndef SENSOR_H /* 1. guard opens */
#define SENSOR_H
#include <stdint.h> /* 2. what we need */
/* 3. declarations only */
void sensor_init(void);
int sensor_read(void);
#endif /* 4. SENSOR_H */
Why guard?
A header may be #included many times. The guard
makes the compiler read its contents only once.
Without it
Duplicate typedefs and prototypes cause
'redefinition' errors.
The pattern
#ifndef / #define at the top, #endif at the bottom —
one unique macro name per header.
14
P R O J E C T S T R U C T U R E
Organising a multi-file project
sensor_monitor/
├─ include/
│ ├─ sensor.h
│ └─ adc.h
├─ src/
│ ├─ main.c
│ ├─ sensor.c
│ └─ adc.c
├─ tests/
│ └─ test_sensor.c
└─ build/
1
Separate interfaces from code
Public headers live in include/, sources in src/.
2
Keep build outputs apart
Object files and binaries go to build/ — never mixed with
source.
3
Mirror tests to modules
One test file per module keeps coverage obvious.
4
Build from the terminal
One gcc command compiles every source into build/.
15
H O W C I S B U I L T
The compilation model
Every .c file is a translation unit that travels through four stages to become machine code.
1
Preprocess
Expand #include & macros
.c → .i
2
Compile
C → assembly
.i → .s
3
Assemble
Assembly → object
.s → .o
4
Link
Combine .o + libs
.o → exe
The compiler sees one .c at a time. It trusts headers for declarations of things defined elsewhere — the linker resolves them at the
end.
16
D E P E N D E N C I E S
Include dependencies & rebuilds
main.c sensor.h
sensor.c adc.h
#include
Headers create edges
When A #includes B, A depends on B.
Change ripples
Edit sensor.h → every .c that includes it must be
recompiled.
Keep graphs shallow
Include only what a file truly needs; prefer forward
declarations.
No cycles
Two headers including each other is a red flag — break
the loop.
17
C O M P I L I N G
Compiling from the terminal
Terminal
$ gcc -c src/main.c -Iinclude
$ gcc -c src/sensor.c -Iinclude
$ gcc -c src/adc.c -Iinclude
$ gcc main.o sensor.o adc.o -o app
$ ./app
# edited sensor.c? recompile just it:
$ gcc -c src/sensor.c -Iinclude
# then relink into the app:
$ gcc main.o sensor.o adc.o -o app
Compile, then link
Turn each .c into a .o, then link the .o files into one
binary.
Recompile only what changed
Re-run gcc -c on the file you edited, then relink — no
full rebuild.
Point at your headers
-Iinclude lets the compiler find your project headers.
Keep warnings on
-Wall -Wextra surface bugs before they ship.

The Program, End to End
We now build one small multi-file program — sensor_monitor —
across four files, compiled from the terminal.
19
W O R K E D E X A M P L E
sensor_monitor — the plan
A tiny program that reads a temperature sensor and warns when it exceeds a limit — split into clean modules.
HEADER
sensor.h
Interface: types + prototypes
for the sensor module.
SOURCE
sensor.c
Implementation: reads ADC,
converts, checks limit.
SOURCE
main.c
Application: drives the loop,
prints results & warnings.
BUILD
gcc
Terminal build: gcc compiles
and links the whole project.
main.c includes sensor.h which sensor.c implements → gcc compiles & links all of it.
20
C O D E · 1 O F 4
sensor.h — the interface
include/sensor.h
#ifndef SENSOR_H
#define SENSOR_H
#include <stdint.h>
typedef struct {
uint16_t raw;
int16_t celsius;
} sensor_reading_t;
void sensor_init(void);
sensor_reading_t sensor_read(void);
int sensor_is_over_limit(int16_t c);
#endif /* SENSOR_H */
Guard
Prevents double inclusion.
Public type
Shared struct the caller can use.
Prototypes only
The contract — no bodies here.
21
C O D E · 2 O F 4
sensor.c — the implementation
src/sensor.c
#include "sensor.h"
#include "adc.h"
#define TEMP_LIMIT_C 105
static uint16_t s_last_raw; /* private */
void sensor_init(void) {
adc_init();
s_last_raw = 0U;
}
sensor_reading_t sensor_read(void) {
sensor_reading_t r;
r.raw = adc_sample(SENSOR_CH);
r.celsius = (r.raw / 4) - 40;
return r;
}
int sensor_is_over_limit(int16_t c) {
return c > TEMP_LIMIT_C;
}
Includes own header
Compiler checks bodies match prototypes.
static = private
s_last_raw is hidden from other files.
Definitions live here
Exactly one .c defines each function.
22
C O D E · 3 O F 4
main.c — using the interface
src/main.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include "sensor.h"
int main(void) {
sensor_init();
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
sensor_reading_t r = sensor_read();
printf("t=%d %d C\n", i, r.celsius);
if (sensor_is_over_limit(r.celsius)) {
printf(" WARNING: over limit!\n");
}
}
return 0;
}
Only needs the header
main never sees sensor.c internals.
Calls the contract
init, read, and the limit check.
Swappable backend
Rewrite sensor.c freely — main is untouched.
23
B U I L D · 4 O F 4
Compile & link from the terminal
Terminal — build
# compile each source to an object
$ gcc -c src/main.c -Iinclude
$ gcc -c src/sensor.c -Iinclude
$ gcc -c src/adc.c -Iinclude
# link the objects into one binary
$ gcc main.o sensor.o adc.o -o app
# run it
$ ./app
$ build & run
$ gcc *.c -o app -Iinclude
cc -c src/main.c ...
cc -c src/sensor.c ...
cc -o app *.o
$ ./app
t=0 23 C
t=1 61 C
t=2 108 C
WARNING: over limit!

D E B U G G I N G
Common multi-file pitfalls & fixes
Multiple definition
Same function/variable defined in two .c
files.
FIX Define once in a .c; only declare in the
.h.
Missing include guard
Header included twice → redefinition
errors.
FIX Wrap every header in #ifndef / #define /
#endif.
Circular includes
Two headers include each other endlessly.
FIX Break the cycle with a forward
declaration.
Leaking internals
Helpers visible to the whole program.
FIX Mark file-local functions & data static.
Undefined reference
Declared, called, but never defined/linked.
FIX Add the .o to the build; check the
linker.
Header bloat
Heavy headers slow every compile.
FIX Include only what's needed; forward-
declare.
25
P R O F E S S I O N A L H A B I T S
Modular design checklist
D E S I G N & S T R U C T U R E
✓One module = one responsibility
✓Keep interfaces small and stable
✓Hide internals with static
✓Include the minimum each file needs
✓Every header has an include guard
R I G O U R & Q U A L I T Y
✓Define each symbol exactly once
✓Prefer const-correct parameters
✓Name files after the module
✓Compile with -Wall; treat warnings as errors
✓One test file per module

I N D U S T R Y C A S E S T U D Y
Inside an ECU: the same ideas, at scale
A Body Control Module can run hundreds of files. The same structure — modules behind
headers — is what keeps it safe, testable, and shippable.
L A Y E R E D , M O D U L A R A R C H I T E C T U R E
Application lighting · wipers · doors · diagnostics
Services state machines · scheduling · fault mgmt
Drivers ADC · PWM · CAN · GPIO modules
HAL / MCAL register-level hardware abstraction
Each layer talks only to the one below, through headers.

Exercises: split & build
ASplit the monolith

Start from a single-file main.c. Move
the add, sub, mul and div functions

CGrow a module

P R A C T I C E · C H E C K Y O U R S E L F
Quick quiz
Q1
Why do headers need include guards?
A To stop the same declarations being read twice → no
redefinition errors.
Q2
What belongs in a .c but never a .h?
A Function definitions (bodies) and static, file-private data.
Q3
Which stage resolves calls between files?
A The linker — it binds each call to its single definition.
Q4
What does 'static' at file scope do?
A Gives internal linkage: the symbol is private to that .c file.
Q5
Header A includes B and B includes A — problem?
A A circular dependency; break it with a forward declaration.
Q6
Edit sensor.h — what must rebuild?
A Every translation unit that #includes sensor.h.

Mini-project: Sensor Data Logger
The brief
Build a medium multi-file C program that reads readings
from multiple sensors, records min / max / average, and
logs alerts when limits are crossed.
SUGGESTED MODULES
sensor — acquire & scale readings
stats — min / max / running average
logger — format & write alert lines
main — wire modules; run the loop
Deliverables
Separate .h / .c per module with include guards
A clean terminal build using gcc -Wall -Wextra
A short README: how to build, run & extend
How it's graded
Modularity & interfaces 40%
Correctness & build hygiene 35%
Readability & docs 25%
